newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Jakarta exchange working to reduce volatility.
newsitem.headline: Jakarta exchange working to reduce volatility.

text.p: The Jakarta Stock Exchange is determined to enhance stability by building a domestic investor base and improving its trading systems, exchange director Felia Salim told delegates to a mutual funds conference on Monday.
"There is volatility, but we are now being given the mandate to go all out to build a domestic investor base to gain overall stability," Salim said.
Public education will form the vanguard of the exchange's efforts to build the domestic market, with more than 40 percent of next year's budget dedicated to public information campaigns, she added.
"Information dissemination is key to speeding up development of the market," Salim said.
The stock exchange faces a formidable task, with surveys revealing that only 17 percent of the population knows what a stock exchange is.

In addition, domestic investors who are aware of the market appear disinclined to invest. Salim said there are 191 licensed and operating pension funds in Indonesia with a combined value of 16.2 trillion rupiah ($6.96 billion) in December 1995.
Only three percent of these funds have invested in the domestic market, even though independent pension consultants estimate their return has averaged 19.6 percent.
Volatility is the prime disincentive to investing in the Jakarta Stock Exchange, which is dominated by four stocks and where foreigners account for 60 percent of trading value.

"Obviously, mutual funds are key to achieving a more sustainable capital market, a more even distribution of trade between foreigners and locals, and hopefully making the equities market less volatile," the exchange director noted.
Attempts to automate trading appear to have been successful, with daily transactions rising to 7,000 a day from 1,000 a day following the introduction of automated trading in May 1995.
Brokers also can trade from desk top computer terminals around Jakarta, and the system soon will be expanded outside the capital.

Scripless trading will be established in April 1997, but will take four years to get fully underway, Salim added. Initial public offerings will be the first to go scripless, followed by inactive stocks.
